rashi:a1.1: And likewise Harim, and likewise Pashḥur, and likewise Immer: and Jehoiarib never again ascended.
rashi:a2.1: Rav Ashi said: Actually, [“and likewise] in the Second” [Temple] refers to the year after the Sabbatical Year, and it is [in accordance with] the Rabbis. And as for what was difficult for you above, that it was destroyed in a Sabbatical Year, this is not difficult: for the first six years from the building of the House until Ezra ascended and sanctified Eretz Yisrael, they did not count Sabbatical Years and Jubilees. Remove six years from the years of the House, and you find year 420 in a Sabbatical Year. How so? Four hundred [years; the printed text adds “and six years” in parentheses] are eight Jubilees, and fourteen years are two Sabbatical cycles; and in year 421, which was the year after a Sabbatical Year, it was destroyed.
rashi:a2.2: And from where do we know that Ezra did not ascend until six years [had passed]? As it is written: “Then ceased,” etc. Evidently the building began in the second year of Darius.
rashi:a3.1: And it is written: “And this house was finished,” etc. Evidently it was completed in year six; that is five years. And at that same time in the following year, which is the sixth year of the building, Ezra ascended and came to Jerusalem in the month of Av; and until Tishrei, which is the seventh [year] of the building, he did not begin to count.
rashi:a7.1: Eighty less two: for from the sending of the spies until they entered the land was only thirty-eight [years], apart from the year of the sending, since they were sent in the second [year] after the exodus from Egypt.
rashi:a8.1: From the fact that you do not find “fourteen years after the city was smitten”: that it should be a Jubilee, unless you subtract fourteen for the conquest and the division.
rashi:a9.1: Mishna. Than nine harps: the reason is not explained.
rashi:a9.2: And the cymbal alone: there was one cymbal there and no more, and the reason is explained in the Gemara.
rashi:a10.1: Gemara. It enters our mind [at first] that he says “sufficient for Shabbat and for the two Festival days” precisely: that for this reason we require six, so that if Shabbat and the two Festival days of Rosh HaShana come together and they cannot inspect, they will have [lambs] ready [Rashi’s word is “rams”].
rashi:a11.1: Refers to the general case: that on all the days of the year as well we require six, and not because of Shabbat and Rosh HaShana, but because of ben Bag Bag, as is explained shortly.
rashi:a11.2: Merely a mnemonic: so that you do not err in the wording and teach four or five; for this reason he mentioned these three days, which require six daily offerings.
tosafot:a1.1: That even if the watch of Jehoiarib ascends: Rashi explains that he never again ascended. And this is puzzling: from where does he know that he never again ascended? It implies that he could ascend, since it says “that even if the watch of Jehoiarib ascends.” Moreover, Rabbeinu Elḥanan asked: many ascended, and it is not clear to us that he did not ascend. And Rabbi [so the text] said: In any case it is possible that Jehoiarib ascended, and here the Gemara is asking this: was the watch of Jehoiarib [one of the watches] in the Second [Temple]? For the twenty-four were these [four families], corresponding to the watches that did not ascend; they were divided into twenty-four watches and served in their place.
tosafot:a2.1: Those six until Ezra ascended and sanctified are not counted: This requires examination according to what I explained, that even when the tribes were exiled they still counted Jubilees in order to sanctify the Sabbatical Years. If so, in the Babylonian exile before Ezra ascended they should also have been counting; why did they begin to count when Ezra ascended? One can say that it is not comparable: certainly while Israel is on its land, even when the Jubilee is not in effect, the Sabbatical Year is in effect with regard to plowing and sowing, and they would sanctify it; but in exile they did not sanctify the Sabbatical Year at all. And this requires examination: even when they were in exile they would need to sanctify the Sabbatical Year because of the remission of debts, which applies both in the land and outside the land. And if it is so that the Sabbatical Year does not depend on the Jubilee, then even when Israel is in exile and not on its land at all, why should they not count Sabbatical cycles, just as when part of Israel is on its land? For even though not all its inhabitants are on it, they count the Sabbatical Year, even though they do not count the Jubilee.
tosafot:a4.1: At that same time in the following year: which is the third [the text adds “and twentieth” in parentheses] of Adar, Ezra ascended from Babylonia, and he arrived at Jerusalem in the fifth month, for he was delayed on the journey from the month of Adar until the month of Av.
tosafot:a7.1: How old was Caleb? Eighty less two: Rabbeinu Elḥanan asked: from where do we know that Caleb was forty years old precisely in the second year, so that when Israel crossed the Jordan he was eighty less two? Perhaps he had begun his forty-first year, and at the sending of the spies he was at the end of his fortieth, for we do not find Caleb’s years [stated]; and then when Israel crossed the Jordan he was eighty less one. So from where does the Talmud know that they conquered for seven and divided for seven? And Rabbi [so the text] said: The verse does not come to obscure but to explain; for why do we need Caleb’s years, if not to inform us with certainty that they conquered for seven and divided for seven?
tosafot:a11.1: What is “sufficient for Shabbat”? Merely a mnemonic: Here it explains from the outset that “sufficient for Shabbat” is merely a mnemonic. But in Menaḥot, chapter HaTekhelet (Menaḥot 49b), it does not say so until the conclusion, where it says: Ravina said to Rav Ashi: These six are seven, for there is the morning of Sunday. [There] it mentioned Shabbat precisely, and this is the explanation: if the two days of Rosh HaShana were on Thursday and Friday, on Sunday they would inspect the daily offering of Thursday, which is four days before its slaughter; and that of Friday, which is the second [day] of Rosh HaShana, they would inspect on Monday, which is four days before its slaughter; and likewise that of Shabbat is inspected on Tuesday. And he asks: they are seven, for there is the morning of Sunday, which also requires inspection four days before its slaughter; and if so, how can they have fewer than seven?
gershom:a1.1: Jehoiarib the head [of the watches]: [it implies that he was the head of all the watches], as is written in Chronicles.
gershom:a2.1: [Actually it is the Rabbis, and actually it was destroyed in the year after the Sabbatical Year. And as for the difficulty, that it would be in the sixth [year] of the Sabbatical cycle, that is not difficult: for those first five years in which they built the Second Temple, until Ezra ascended and sanctified Sabbatical Years and Jubilees, are not counted, as it is written: “Then ceased,” until the second year of Darius; as it is written: “And this house was finished on the third day of the month Adar, which was the sixth year of the reign of Darius.”
gershom:a3.1: And at that same time in the following year Ezra ascended from Babylonia: evidently there were six years in which Ezra did not ascend. And it is written: “And he came to Jerusalem in the fifth month, which was the seventh year of the king.” This teaches that from the seventh [year] onward he began to sanctify.
gershom:a4.1: When Israel crossed the Jordan, at the end of the forty years that they were in the wilderness, Caleb was seventy-eight years old.
gershom:a5.1: From the fact that you do not find fourteen years after the city was smitten [to be a] Jubilee, unless you also count the seven years in which they divided.]
gershom:a6.1: That are inspected: for a blemish.
gershom:a7.1: Sufficient for Shabbat and for the two Festival days.
gershom:a8.1: There are many: for Shabbat and the two Festival days of Rosh HaShana many lambs are needed for the daily offerings and additional offerings, and six do not suffice.
rashi:b1.1: Four days before slaughter: and for this reason we always require six. At the time of inauguration they placed there six [lambs] inspected four days before. On the first day they took two for the daily offerings and put two in their place, and inspected them; on the second day they took two of the remaining four and put two in their place; and on the third day they took the two that remained of the first ones and put two in their place. And so always they take two and put two; and those that were inspected and placed there on the first day are fit for the fourth day, and those placed on the second are fit for the fifth, and so they go around forever. Thus all the daily offerings that are slaughtered are inspected four days before slaughter, counting the day of inspection and the day of slaughter. So I heard. But it is difficult for me: this is not comparable to the four days of the Paschal offering, whose inspection is on the tenth and its slaughter on the fourteenth, which is four days apart from the day of slaughter. Therefore it seems to me that eight were placed there on the day of inauguration, and the “six” taught in the mishna means this: one does not have fewer than six; that is, even when they take the two of each day, six inspected ones remain there. And afterward, before nightfall, they inspect two and place them there; and those, since they are not yet there at the time the two are taken, are not counted. Another version: merely a mnemonic: just as when Shabbat and Rosh HaShana fall next to each other, the [lamb] for Tuesday is inspected on Friday, since on those days they cannot go and seek out a lamb and inspect it, so that it is then four days before slaughter, so too we always require four days before slaughter.
rashi:b3.1: It is also precise: that it is merely a mnemonic, and that he does not require them because of Shabbat and Rosh HaShana: since it does not teach “for Shabbat and for the two days,” etc., which would imply for the needs of Shabbat and Rosh HaShana. Since it teaches “sufficient,” learn from it [that it means] according to the count appropriate for Shabbat and Rosh HaShana, which is six, and it is merely a mnemonic.
rashi:b5.1: From where is this matter derived: that there is a cymbal alone and no more.
rashi:b5.2: And Asaph: the name of the Levite.
rashi:b5.3: They perform one act: for one is of no use without its fellow; they are two broad pieces of metal, and one strikes them against each other (Rashi adds an Old French gloss).
rashi:b6.1: Mishna. A minor Levite does not enter the courtyard for any service, such as sweeping the courtyard and closing the doors, except at the time when the Levites stand on the platform in song; then minor Levites enter to sing with them.
rashi:b6.2: And they would not: those minors.
rashi:b6.3: Say with a lyre and a harp, but with the mouth, in order to provide flavor to the music: to put spice into the pleasantness of the Levites, because the voice of the minor Levites is fine and it seasons the voice of the adult Levites.
rashi:b7.1: [And they are not tallied in the count]: that those Levites are not counted in the count of twelve Levites needed for the platform.
rashi:b7.2: And they do not ascend: onto the bench prepared for the platform; rather, they would stand on the ground.
rashi:b7.3: And cadets [tzoarei] of the Levites: for they cause the Levites anguish [metza’arin], as is explained in the Gemara.
rashi:b13.1: Gemara. With the ten-stringed lyre [nevel asor]: of ten strings. And it is speaking of the World-to-Come, since it is written “a new song [shir ḥadash],” in the masculine form; for the songs of this world are in the feminine form [shira], as is said in the Mekhilta: just as a female gives birth, so these salvations are destined to give birth to troubles. But the song of the World-to-Come is in the masculine form, as it does not give birth.
rashi:b14.1: Since Rabbi Yehuda derives the harp [kinor] from “the ten-stringed lyre [nevel asor],” evidently a harp is a lyre.
rashi:b14.2: Its sound is increased like a lyre: and a lyre [nevel] is made like a blacksmith’s bellows and produces its sound by means of air.
rashi:b15.2: The Levites’ voices are thick. The minors’ voices are thin: their voice is fine.
rashi:b15.3: Mekatetei: that is, they make [their voice] small, making it very fine and beautiful; and they cause the Levites anguish, since they cannot sweeten their voice like theirs.
rashi:b17.1: Mishna. To be lenient: [heading; explained with the next comment].
rashi:b17.2: To be stringent: for one who valuates the most unsightly among the Jewish people, even if he is worth only five sela, gives fifty sela, [for one] from twenty until sixty years old.
rashi:b17.3: With regard to an ancestral field: with regard to one who consecrates an ancestral field.
rashi:b18.1: The most attractive among the Jewish people: who is worth a hundred maneh; he gives only fifty sela.
rashi:b18.2: Who took a vow of valuation: who said: The valuation of so-and-so is upon me.
rashi:b19.1: Gemara. With regard to gentiles, no: that if a Jew said, The valuation of so-and-so the gentile is upon me, he has said nothing, since a gentile is not valuated.
rashi:b20.1: Is valuated but does not take a vow of valuation: the reason is explained in the first chapter (above, Arakhin 5b).
tosafot:b4.1: And one may add up to an infinite number; until how many? Rav Huna said, and some say, etc.: And Rabbi [so the text] said: It is certainly obvious that one may add infinitely. Rather, he asks: until how many is it an enhancement of the mitzva, so that one need not search further for priests? Rav Huna said: Up to 120, for we find in the verse (II Chronicles 5) that they sought out 120 priests to blow trumpets, and no more. Alternatively: it is obvious that one does not add infinitely, for if they added more there would be a jumble of sound. Rav Huna said: One may add up to 120 priests, for we find in the verse that we are not concerned about a jumble of sound [with that many].
tosafot:b6.1: No fewer than twelve Levites standing on the platform: every day when they say the song: two lyres and nine harps and a cymbal, that makes twelve. And the two trumpets: priests blow them, and not Levites. And so we learned in the last chapter of Tamid (33b): “And two priests stand at the table of the fats with two trumpets in their hands.” And there it did not bother to teach the harps and the flutes, because they were played not by priests but by Levites. And it is slightly difficult, since it teaches there: “And ben Arza struck the cymbal.” And he answered that it mentioned one of them.
tosafot:b9.1: A minor does not enter the courtyard; from where is this matter derived? Rabbi Yoḥanan said: As the verse states: “Then stood Jeshua, his sons and his brethren, Kadmiel”: Rabbeinu Elḥanan asked: How do we derive that a minor enters the courtyard for song at a time when the Levites stand on the platform? And Ri said that he includes it from a superfluity in the verse. It is written: “their sons and their brethren the Levites,” and it is written: “Jeshua, his sons…Kadmiel and his sons, the sons of Judah, the sons of Ḥenadad” [the printed text reads “Morad,” corrected in brackets to “Ḥenadad”]. Why do I need “their sons”? Hasn’t it already mentioned each one’s sons? Rather, learn from it that it was written for this, since it is superfluous, and it implies minors.
tosafot:b17.1: Yesh BaArakhin [Tosafot’s heading for the new chapter, with no comment of its own here].
tosafot:b17.2: (This belongs to 14a.) What is the difference between a purchased field and an ancestral field, etc.: And similarly, it could have stated another difference between an ancestral field and a purchased field: with an ancestral field, if he consecrated it and another redeemed it, it is divided among the priests at the Jubilee; and with a purchased field, if he consecrated it and another redeemed it, it returns to the [original] owners at the Jubilee. But it chose to explain only a difference that applies when he himself redeems it.
gershom:b1.1: Refers to the general case: to ordinary weekdays, and he refers to the daily offerings alone. And what he says, “sufficient for Shabbat and for the two Festival days,” is merely a mnemonic, that there must be six daily-offering lambs [inspected every day in the chamber. What is the reason? So that on each day of the week they may slaughter two daily offerings] that were inspected four days before slaughter. How so? On the first day [of the week] there were six inspected; he slaughtered two of them on the first day and brought two in their place; there remained four inspected and two not inspected, which makes six. On the second day he slaughters two of the inspected and brings two others in their place; [on the third day he slaughters two inspected and brings two others in their place.] Those he brought on the first day in place of those he slaughtered are fit to be offered on the fourth day, for they have been inspected four days, and part of the fourth day is like all of it; and those he brought on the second day are fit for the fifth day, and those of the third day for the sixth, and those of the fourth day for Shabbat, [and those of the fifth day for the first day,] and so it goes around; and every day there are two inspected [for slaughter]. Therefore one has no fewer than six inspected lambs in the chamber.
gershom:b2.1: With the cymbals [metziltayim]: this is the cymbal [tziltzal].
gershom:b3.1: [Since they perform one act, and one man strikes one against the other, they call them one cymbal.]
gershom:b4.1: As it is stated: “he and his brethren and sons were twelve”: for the Levites were divided into twenty-four watches, corresponding to the twenty-four priestly watches, and each watch received twelve, as is written in Chronicles of each one: “he and his brethren and sons were twelve.” And when you combine them all, each watch comes to twelve.
gershom:b5.1: A minor does not: [enter], a Levite.
gershom:b6.1: Enter the courtyard for service: for song.
gershom:b7.1: Except at the time when the Levites: the adults stand [in song], for the minor Levites would enter to assist the Levites in the song.
gershom:b8.1: And those children would not say the song:
gershom:b9.1: Not with a lyre and not with a harp, but with the mouth, in order to provide flavor to the music: that is, because the voice of the children is fine, their voice would make the song pleasant, like spices that make food pleasant.
gershom:b10.1: As it is stated: “his sons”; and the sons of Judah were minors. This teaches that all of them led in song, adults and minors.
gershom:b11.1: “With an instrument of ten strings [asor] and with the lyre [nevel]”: that is, it had [ten] strings.
gershom:b12.1: And it says: “Give thanks unto the Lord with the harp; with the lyre of ten strings,” and it is not written “and with the lyre”; evidently [he holds] that they are one.
gershom:b13.1: Since its strings are increased: of the harp in the World-to-Come.
gershom:b14.1: Its sound is increased like a lyre: that lyre which is covered with the skin of the belly; he calls it a lyre.
gershom:b15.1: [They are not tallied in the count: that child is not tallied in the count of twelve Levites.
gershom:b16.1: And they do not stand on the platform: in that high place where the Levites stand.
gershom:b17.1: And helpers [soadei] of the Levites: those who assist the Levites in the song.
gershom:b18.1: These: the minors are mekatetei, they make their voices small, for their voice is fine; and those, the adults, do not make their voices small, for their voice is thick. Therefore they call them tze’irei [the young ones] of the Levites.] [So Rabbeinu Gershom’s text, reading “tze’irei” rather than “tzoarei.”]
gershom:b19.1: We will return to you, Ein Ne’erakhin.
gershom:b20.1: Yesh BaArakhin [to be lenient and to be stringent: that if he valuated the most attractive among the Jewish people, he gives only fifty sela.
gershom:b21.1: And to be stringent: that if he valuated the most unsightly among the Jewish people, he also gives fifty sela.
gershom:b22.1: One who consecrates his field] in the sandy area of Meḥoza [this explains the continuation of the mishna on 14a]: that is, a field near the city’s outskirts, which people tread upon; and moreover, since it is near the city and stands with its standing grain, [people] see it and cast an evil eye upon it, and it does not produce so much fruit.
gershom:b23.1: With regard to a Jew, yes: that is, it teaches “the most attractive among the Jewish people,” and it does not teach “the most attractive among gentiles.” Let us say that the mishna, etc.
